claims.text: The initial alloy is a high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents and three additional elements at 5–35 at% each.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous, equiaxed grain structure.
Adding 2 at% yttrium to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
Oxidizing exposure between 600°C and 800°C will promote in situ oxidation of yttrium.
The intervention will produce finely dispersed Y2O3 particles at grain boundaries and within grains.
Yttrium will oxidize preferentially under the specified high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The resulting Y2O3 particles will be stable and nanometer-scale.
Y2O3 dispersoids will pin grain boundaries and retard grain-boundary sliding.
Y2O3 dispersoids will inhibit dislocation motion.
Retarding grain-boundary sliding and inhibiting dislocation motion will increase creep resistance and high-temperature strength.
At 700°C, the yttrium-doped alloy will have a lower creep rate than the undoped control.
At 700°C, the yttrium-doped alloy will have higher tensile strength than the undoped control.
The expected improvement in elevated-temperature performance is approximately 10–30%.
Oxide-dispersion strengthening is well established in other alloy families such as ODS steels.
The quantitative effect and stability of oxide-dispersion strengthening are not well characterized in titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys.
Variation in oxide-particle size, distribution, and matrix interactions may alter the magnitude of the mechanical-property improvement.
